meta.headline: Is there a secret Treasury account in your name that can pay off your debts?
meta.seoTitle: Birth certificate bonds and the secret Treasury account

dek.text: The Treasury says the accounts that redemption kits tell people to draw on do not exist, and a federal court treated a bill drawn on one as a worthless piece of paper.

description.text: The Treasury says the secret accounts behind birth certificate bonds do not exist. What courts did with the bills, and what the gold law says.

assertions.text: The Treasury says the claimed accounts "are fictitious and do not exist in the Treasury system".

sections.name: hook
sections.heading: A mortgage bill drawn on a secret account

sentences.text: In Virginia, a borrower tried to clear her home loan by sending Washington Mutual a $244,663.79 bill of exchange, drawn on what she called a contract trust account administered through the IRS.

assertions.text: In Bryant v. Washington Mutual, the plaintiff tried to pay off her mortgage with a $244,663.79 bill of exchange drawn on a contract trust account she said was administered through the IRS.

sentences.text: Her complaint reasoned that because the bank had received the bill, "this loan is paid off".

assertions.text: In Bryant v. Washington Mutual, the plaintiff concluded that since the bill of exchange was received at the location the lender designated, "this loan is paid off".

quote.text: this loan is paid off

blocks.caption: The bill of exchange the borrower sent her lender, as her complaint described it.

sentences.text: This article follows the story her bill relied on, step by step, from the name on a birth certificate to the account it is meant to fund, and then the older idea underneath it, that leaving gold made debts impossible to pay.
Each step is set against what the Treasury, the IRS and the courts have said about it.

sections.name: question-1
sections.heading: Is there really a secret Treasury account in my name that can pay off my debts?

sentences.text: Believers say the account belongs to a second, legal version of you; in the words of jonhoyle.com, "The all capitals spelling of the name creates a corporate fiction".

assertions.text: jonhoyle.com says "The all capitals spelling of the name creates a corporate fiction".

quote.text: The all capitals spelling of the name creates a corporate fiction
quote.speaker: jonhoyle.com

sentences.text: The birth certificate is said to give that fiction its value, with the site Understand Contract Law claiming "These birth certificate bonds have a value and are being traded".

assertions.text: Understand Contract Law says "These birth certificate bonds have a value and are being traded".

quote.text: These birth certificate bonds have a value and are being traded
quote.speaker: Understand Contract Law

sentences.text: The proceeds are supposed to be reachable: jonhoyle.com describes "an alphanumeric account number in your Strawman name that is your private account that can be drawn from", and a YouTube tutorial calls a stamped Social Security number on a bill "what's going to give you access into your treasury account".

assertions.text: jonhoyle.com says "there is an alphanumeric account number in your Strawman name that is your private account that can be drawn from".

quote.text: an alphanumeric account number in your Strawman name that is your private account that can be drawn from
quote.speaker: jonhoyle.com

assertions.text: A YouTube tutorial says the stamp with your social security number is "what's going to give you access into your treasury account".

quote.text: what's going to give you access into your treasury account

sentences.text: On the account, the Treasury is direct: such accounts "are fictitious and do not exist in the Treasury system".

assertions.text: The Treasury says the claimed accounts "are fictitious and do not exist in the Treasury system".

quote.text: are fictitious and do not exist in the Treasury system
quote.speaker: Treasury

sentences.text: The IRS, citing the Sixth Circuit in United States v. Anderson, adds that the Treasury "does not maintain depository accounts against which an individual can draw a check, draft, or any other financial instrument", adding that "The notion of secret accounts assigned to each citizen is pure fantasy".

assertions.text: The IRS quotes the Sixth Circuit in United States v. Anderson: the Treasury "does not maintain depository accounts against which an individual can draw a check, draft, or any other financial instrument".

quote.text: does not maintain depository accounts against which an individual can draw a check, draft, or any other financial instrument
quote.speaker: Sixth Circuit

assertions.text: The IRS says "The notion of secret accounts assigned to each citizen is pure fantasy".

quote.text: The notion of secret accounts assigned to each citizen is pure fantasy
quote.speaker: IRS

sentences.text: The Treasury also notes that some websites sell videos, webinars and coaching on these methods, and that "No one has profited from the Treasury Department by using these tactics".

assertions.text: The Treasury says some internet sites sell videos, webinars and coaching on birth-certificate bond schemes, and "No one has profited from the Treasury Department by using these tactics".

quote.text: No one has profited from the Treasury Department by using these tactics
quote.speaker: Treasury

sentences.text: Nor is the birth certificate an asset: according to the Treasury, "There is no monetary value to a birth certificate", and it cannot be used to make purchases.

assertions.text: The Treasury says "There is no monetary value to a birth certificate" and that birth certificates cannot be used for purchases.

quote.text: There is no monetary value to a birth certificate
quote.speaker: Treasury

sentences.text: When a claimant in Gravatt v. United States argued that his birth certificate was a contract with the government, the Court of Federal Claims called the claim frivolous, holding that such documents do not "recognize or impose contractual rights, obligations, or duties".

assertions.text: In Gravatt v. United States the Court of Federal Claims held the claim that a birth certificate and social security number are express contracts with the United States frivolous; they do not "recognize or impose contractual rights, obligations, or duties".

quote.text: recognize or impose contractual rights, obligations, or duties
quote.speaker: Gravatt v. United States

sentences.text: The same court doubted the Treasury trust fund he said he was owed from, writing that it "strains all logic and reason to believe that the trust fund alleged by plaintiff actually exists".

assertions.text: Gravatt claimed to fall within the Treasury trust-fund statutes; the court said it "strains all logic and reason to believe that the trust fund alleged by plaintiff actually exists".

quote.text: strains all logic and reason to believe that the trust fund alleged by plaintiff actually exists

sentences.text: The split person at the start of the chain fares no better: a legal history of these movements in Canada says the strawman "has no basis in law in either the US or Canada", and the Supreme Court of Queensland found it "does not find any reflection in any provision of our law".

assertions.text: Netolitzky's history of these movements in Canada says the strawman concept "has no basis in law in either the US or Canada".

quote.text: has no basis in law in either the US or Canada

assertions.text: The Supreme Court of Queensland, in Borleis v Wacol Correctional Centre, said the strawman argument "does not find any reflection in any provision of our law".

quote.text: does not find any reflection in any provision of our law
quote.speaker: Supreme Court of Queensland

sentences.text: The case against the strawman here rests on legal commentary and individual rulings from the United States, Canada and Australia, not on a survey of every court that has heard it.

assertions.text: Netolitzky's history of these movements in Canada says the strawman concept "has no basis in law in either the US or Canada".
The Supreme Court of Queensland, in Borleis v Wacol Correctional Centre, said the strawman argument "does not find any reflection in any provision of our law".

sentences.text: The strongest of it is Canadian: a study of applications to the Supreme Court of Canada concludes that the strawman is incompatible with Canadian law and that "Any human being is a legal person".

assertions.text: Netolitzky and Warman conclude from Supreme Court of Canada leave applications that the strawman theory is incompatible with Canadian law and "Any human being is a legal person".

quote.text: Any human being is a legal person

sentences.text: Every source here rejects the idea, but the record grades these sources short of the level it treats as settled, so the claim is listed as studied rather than closed.

That leaves the instrument itself, and the Treasury's verdict is that "All these Bills of Exchange drawn on the U.S. Treasury are worthless", adding that drawing such drafts on it "is fraudulent and a violation of federal law".

assertions.text: The Treasury says "All these Bills of Exchange drawn on the U.S. Treasury are worthless".

quote.text: All these Bills of Exchange drawn on the U.S. Treasury are worthless
quote.speaker: Treasury

qualifications: s23 says these sources do not count how often ordinary users are charged.

assertions.text: The Treasury says drawing such drafts on the U.S. Treasury "is fraudulent and a violation of federal law".

quote.text: is fraudulent and a violation of federal law
quote.speaker: Treasury

qualifications: s23 says these sources do not count how often ordinary users are charged.

sentences.text: Courts outside the US have reached the same view: in Bosse v. Farm Credit Canada, a family claimed to have settled debts on wood lots with setoff bonds drawn on secret US Treasury accounts, and the New Brunswick Court of Appeal found the strategy frivolous and illogical, adding that the family knew it.

assertions.text: In Bosse v. Farm Credit Canada the Bosses claimed they had satisfied debts on wood lots financed by Farm Credit Canada with setoff bonds drawn from secret accounts operated by the US Treasury; the court found the strategy frivolous, without merit and illogical, and said they knew this.

sentences.text: The Virginia borrower fared the same way: her bank called the bill an unacceptable form of payment and foreclosed, and when she sued, the court held that she "did not tender payment, but rather a worthless piece of paper", though it accepted that her belief in the process appeared genuine.

assertions.text: Washington Mutual told the plaintiff the bill of exchange was an unacceptable form of payment, found the borrowers in default and foreclosed on the property.
The court found she "did not tender payment, but rather a worthless piece of paper".

quote.text: did not tender payment, but rather a worthless piece of paper

qualifications: s23 says these sources do not count how often ordinary users are charged.

assertions.text: The court said her belief in the redemption process appears genuine.

sentences.text: Passing these bills can also lead to a criminal case: Barton Buhtz, the promoter whose redemption advice the borrower had relied on, was convicted in Oregon with several co-defendants of fraud charges over passing bills of exchange.

assertions.text: Barton A. Buhtz, whose redemption advice the plaintiff relied on, was convicted in Oregon with several co-defendants of criminal fraud charges related to passing Bills of Exchange.
qualifications: s23 says these sources do not count how often ordinary users are charged.

sentences.text: And in United States v. Heath, the Sixth Circuit upheld the conviction of a man who sent the IRS a so-called "Registered Bill of Exchange", made to look like a certified check with no actual account behind it.

assertions.text: In United States v. Heath the Sixth Circuit affirmed a conviction under 18 USC 514(a) for sending the IRS a so-called "Registered Bill of Exchange" that appeared to be a certified check but had no actual account.

quote.text: Registered Bill of Exchange
quote.speaker: IRS

qualifications: s23 says these sources do not count how often ordinary users are charged.

sentences.text: What these sources record are convictions of a promoter and of people who made or passed the instruments; none of them counts how often an ordinary person who sends a bill to a lender is charged.

assertions.text: Bryant records the fraud conviction of the promoter Buhtz and co-defendants for passing bills of exchange.
The IRS lists appeals that upheld convictions for presenting or passing fictitious instruments drawn on the Treasury (Heath, Getzschman).

sentences.text: So the answer is no: the Treasury says the account is nonexistent, and every court in this evidence that weighed a bill drawn on it found it worthless or frivolous.

assertions.text: The Treasury says the TreasuryDirect accounts the drafts are drawn on are nonexistent.
Bryant found the bill a worthless piece of paper and notes other courts addressing nearly identical claims found likewise.
qualifications: s23 says these sources do not count how often ordinary users are charged.

assertions.text: The New Brunswick Court of Appeal found the A4V setoff bonds frivolous and without merit.
qualifications: s23 says these sources do not count how often ordinary users are charged.

sections.name: question-2
sections.heading: But since the US left gold in 1933, isn't money just credit, so a debt can only be discharged, never paid?

sentences.text: Underneath the account sits an older claim about money, which Educated in Law sums up as "As a result of HJR 192, the people can no longer pay their debts."

assertions.text: Educated in Law says "As a result of HJR 192, the people can no longer pay their debts."

quote.text: As a result of HJR 192, the people can no longer pay their debts.
quote.speaker: Educated in Law

sentences.text: A YouTube video, Take Back Your Strawman Birth Certificate Bonds, says the resolution "eliminated our ability to pay our debts allowing only for their discharge".

assertions.text: The video Take Back Your Strawman Birth Certificate Bonds says the resolution "eliminated our ability to pay our debts allowing only for their discharge".

quote.text: eliminated our ability to pay our debts allowing only for their discharge
quote.speaker: Take Back Your Strawman Birth Certificate Bonds

sentences.text: House Joint Resolution 192 is a real law of 1933, and the court in the Virginia mortgage case read it: its heading is "To assure uniform value to the coins and currencies of the United States".

assertions.text: Bryant reads House Joint Resolution 192 (73d Cong., 1933), headed "To assure uniform value to the coins and currencies of the United States".

quote.text: To assure uniform value to the coins and currencies of the United States

sentences.text: In the court's summary, the resolution voids contract terms that demand payment in gold and makes US currency "legal tender for all debts", the reverse of what the claim needs.

assertions.text: As Bryant reads it, HJR 192 says obligations requiring payment in gold are against public policy and US currency is "legal tender for all debts".

quote.text: legal tender for all debts

sentences.text: The Supreme Court case the borrower also cited, Guaranty Trust Co. v. Henwood, said the resolution ties a debt to the "actual number of dollars promised, dollar for dollar".

assertions.text: Bryant notes the plaintiff also cited Guaranty Trust Co. v. Henwood (1939), in which the Court said obligations are measured by the "actual number of dollars promised, dollar for dollar".

quote.text: actual number of dollars promised, dollar for dollar

sentences.text: The judge concluded that both authorities concern "nothing more than the U.S. monetary shift away from the gold standard" and say nothing of secret trust accounts or bills of exchange.

assertions.text: Bryant says HJR 192 and Henwood "address nothing more than the U.S. monetary shift away from the gold standard" and mention neither secret trust accounts nor Bills of Exchange.

quote.text: nothing more than the U.S. monetary shift away from the gold standard

sentences.text: Paper money settles debts as well: the Eighth Circuit, in United States v. Rifen, held that "Congress has declared federal reserve notes legal tender".

assertions.text: In United States v. Rifen (8th Cir. 1978) the court said "Congress has declared federal reserve notes legal tender".

quote.text: Congress has declared federal reserve notes legal tender

sentences.text: The Ninth Circuit, in United States v. Condo, called "frivolous" the argument that Federal Reserve Notes "are not valid currency, cannot be taxed, and are merely" debts.

assertions.text: In United States v. Condo the Ninth Circuit upheld a criminal tax conviction, rejecting as "frivolous" the argument that Federal Reserve Notes "are not valid currency, cannot be taxed, and are merely" debts.

quote.text: are not valid currency, cannot be taxed, and are merely
quote.speaker: Ninth Circuit

sentences.text: The reading of the resolution itself in this evidence comes from the court in Bryant, a suit over a single mortgage; the appeals rulings here are about Federal Reserve Notes as legal tender in tax cases, not about the resolution.

assertions.text: Bryant reads HJR 192 as addressing the shift away from gold and making US currency legal tender for all debts.
Federal Reserve Notes are legal tender, and circuits reject the claim that they are merely debts.

sentences.text: Both point the same way, but the record grades them short of the level it treats as settled, so the claim stays listed as studied rather than closed.
On what is here, the answer is no: the move off gold changed what stands behind a dollar, while the law kept dollars as payment for any debt.

assertions.text: Bryant reads HJR 192 as addressing the shift away from gold and making US currency legal tender for all debts.
Federal Reserve Notes are legal tender, and circuits reject the claim that they are merely debts.

sentences.text: The Treasury's own account of the scheme begins with the move off gold, and the judge who read that law found it gives the redemption claim "absolutely no support".

assertions.text: The Treasury's summary of the scheme begins "When the United States went off the gold standard in 1933".
Bryant says HJR 192 provides "absolutely no support" for the redemption claim.

quote.text: absolutely no support

sentences.text: A payment method that only works if the Treasury is secretly holding your money is, to a lender, no payment at all.
Whoever sells the method should be able to name a court that accepted it; the rulings above did not.
